2. [MATH: \dfrac{6}{12}]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
A fraction is equivalent to [MATH: \dfrac12] if its numerator is one-half of its denominator.

From the given options, the only fraction where the numerator is not one-half of its denominator is [MATH: \dfrac{\color{red}6}{\color{blue}8}.] Notice that [MATH: {\color{blue}8} \div 2 = 4 \neq {\color{red}6}.]

The symbol [MATH: \neq] means "is not equal to."

We can also represent this visually using a fraction model.

Notice that the shaded areas are not the same. Therefore, the fractions are not equal.

Determine which of the following symbols could replace the empty box above to make the statement true.

1. [MATH: >]
2. [MATH: <]
3. [MATH: =]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
When comparing fractions to [MATH: \dfrac12,] we recall the following:

  • A fraction is greater than [MATH: \dfrac12] if its numerator is greater than one-half of its denominator.

  • A fraction is less than [MATH: \dfrac12] if its numerator is less than one-half of its denominator.

We wish to compare [MATH: \dfrac{\color{red}{3}}{\color{blue}{4}}] to [MATH: \dfrac12.] In this case,

  • the numerator is [MATH: {\color{red}{3}},]

  • the denominator is [MATH: {\color{blue}{4}},]

  • one-half of the denominator is [MATH: {\color{blue}{4}} \div 2 = {\color{purple}{2}}.]

So, the numerator is greater than one-half of the denominator:

[MATH: {\color{red}{3}} > {\color{purple}{2}}]

Therefore, we conclude that

[MATH: \dfrac{\color{red}{3}}{\color{blue}{4}} > \dfrac12.]

We can also represent this comparison using a fraction model:

The fraction on the left has [MATH: \color{blue}3] shaded parts, while the fraction on the right has [MATH: \color{purple}2] shaded parts. Therefore, the fraction on the left is larger.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let's compare each fraction to [MATH: \dfrac12\mathbin{:}]

  • The fraction [MATH: \dfrac {\color{red}{2}} {\color{blue}{3}}] is greater than [MATH: \dfrac 1 2] because [MATH: {\color{red}{2}}] is greater than [MATH: {\color{blue}{3}}\div 2 = 1\,\textrm{R}1 = 1\,\dfrac12.]

  • The fraction [MATH: \dfrac{\color{red}{4}} {\color{blue}{9}}] is less than [MATH: \dfrac 1 2] because [MATH: {\color{red}{4}}] is less than [MATH: {\color{blue}{9}}\div 2 = 4\,\textrm{R}1 = 4\,\dfrac{1}{2}.]

Since [MATH: \dfrac{2}{3}] is greater than [MATH: \dfrac12,] but [MATH: \dfrac{4}{9}] is less than [MATH: \dfrac12,] this means that [MATH: \dfrac{2}{3}] is greater than [MATH: \dfrac{4}{9}\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: \dfrac{2}{3} > \dfrac{4}{9}]

So, the correct answer is "I only."

- The fraction [MATH: \dfrac{\color{red}{4}} {\color{blue}{9}}] is less than [MATH: \dfrac 1 2] because [MATH: {\color{red}{4}}] is less than [MATH: {\color{blue}{9}}\div 2 = 4\,\textrm{R}1 = 4\,\dfrac{1}{2}.]

[IMG: /graphics/eddfa04fce494e33d85236e9109fb06b]

Since [MATH: \dfrac{2}{3}] is greater than [MATH: \dfrac12,] but [MATH: \dfrac{4}{9}] is less than [MATH: \dfrac12,] this means that [MATH: \dfrac{2}{3}] is greater than [MATH: \dfrac{4}{9}\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: \dfrac{2}{3} > \dfrac{4}{9}]

So, the correct answer is "I only."

[IMG: /graphics/90396ad6e626255fc250d8df032b4085]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A fraction is equivalent to [MATH: \dfrac12] if its numerator is one-half of its denominator.

Content:
For example, the following fractions are all equivalent to [MATH: \dfrac12\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\color{red}2}{\color{blue}4}, \qquad \dfrac{\color{red}3}{\color{blue}6}, \qquad \dfrac{\color{red}9}{\color{blue}18}]

Content:
These fractions are equivalent to [MATH: \dfrac12] because when we divide the denominator by [MATH: 2,] we get the numerator:

Content:
- [MATH: \dfrac{\color{red}2}{\color{blue}4}] is equivalent to one-half because [MATH: {\color{blue}{4}} \div 2 = {\color{red}{2}}]
- [MATH: \dfrac{\color{red}3}{\color{blue}6}] is equivalent to one-half because [MATH: {\color{blue}{6}} \div 2 = {\color{red}{3}}]
- [MATH: \dfrac{\color{red}9}{\color{blue}18}] is equivalent to one-half because [MATH: {\color{blue}{18}} \div 2 = {\color{red}{9}}]

Content:
Learning to quickly recognize fractions equivalent to [MATH: \dfrac12] is a valuable skill.

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying Fractions Equivalent to One-Half

Example Prompt:
Which of the following fractions is NOT equivalent to [MATH: \dfrac12?]

1. [MATH: \dfrac{4}{8}]
2. [MATH: \dfrac{6}{12}]
3. [MATH: \dfrac{6}{8}]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
A fraction is equivalent to [MATH: \dfrac12] if its numerator is one-half of its denominator.

From the given options, the only fraction where the numerator is not one-half of its denominator is [MATH: \dfrac{\color{red}6}{\color{blue}8}.] Notice that
[MATH: {\color{blue}8} \div 2 = 4 \neq {\color{red}6}.]

The symbol [MATH: \neq] means "is not equal to."

We can also represent this visually using a fraction model.

[IMG: /graphics/9ed106645c321da904ed597ef9b6c446]

Notice that the shaded areas are not the same. Therefore, the fractions are not equal.

---

Item 5 — Tutorial: Comparing Fractions to One-Half

Content:
Let's consider the following fraction:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\color{red}{2}}{\color{blue}{8}}]

Content:
Is this fraction greater than or less than [MATH: \dfrac12?]

Content:
To answer this question, we notice the following:

Content:
- the numerator is [MATH: {\color{red}{2}}]
- the denominator is [MATH: {\color{blue}{8}}]
- one-half of the denominator is [MATH: {\color{blue}{8}} \div 2 = {\color{purple}{4}}]

Content:
So, the numerator is less than one-half of the denominator:

Content:
[MATH: {\color{red}{2}} < {\color{purple}{4}}]

Content:
Therefore, we conclude that

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\color{red}{2}}{\color{blue}{8}} < \dfrac12.]

Content:
We can also represent this comparison using a fraction model:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/10419da60e42f7ceca1031bf312ca3b9]

Content:
The fraction on the left has [MATH: \color{blue}2] shaded parts, while the fraction on the right has [MATH: \color{purple}4] shaded parts. Therefore, the fraction on the left is smaller.

---

Item 6 — Tutorial: A Rule for Comparing Fractions to One-Half

Content:
In general, we have the following handy rule to compare fractions to [MATH: \dfrac12{:}]

Content:
- A fraction is greater than [MATH: \dfrac12] if its numerator is greater than one-half its denominator.
- A fraction is less than [MATH: \dfrac12] if its numerator is less than one-half its denominator.

Content:
After some practice, you'll be able to spot whether a fraction is greater than or less than [MATH: \dfrac12] quickly.

---

Item 7 — Example: Comparing Fractions to One-Half

Example Prompt:
[MATH: \dfrac{3}{4}\,\square \,\dfrac 1 2]

Determine which of the following symbols could replace the empty box above to make the statement true.

1. [MATH: >]
2. [MATH: <]
3. [MATH: =]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
When comparing fractions to [MATH: \dfrac12,] we recall the following:

- A fraction is greater than [MATH: \dfrac12] if its numerator is greater than one-half of its denominator.
- A fraction is less than [MATH: \dfrac12] if its numerator is less than one-half of its denominator.

We wish to compare [MATH: \dfrac{\color{red}{3}}{\color{blue}{4}}] to [MATH: \dfrac12.] In this case,

- the numerator is [MATH: {\color{red}{3}},]
- the denominator is [MATH: {\color{blue}{4}},]
- one-half of the denominator is [MATH: {\color{blue}{4}} \div 2 = {\color{purple}{2}}.]

So, the numerator is greater than one-half of the denominator:

[MATH: {\color{red}{3}} > {\color{purple}{2}}]

Therefore, we conclude that

[MATH: \dfrac{\color{red}{3}}{\color{blue}{4}} > \dfrac12.]

We can also represent this comparison using a fraction model:

[IMG: /graphics/67c6ba7641613c3e030e8940e2f4b687]

The fraction on the left has [MATH: \color{blue}3] shaded parts, while the fraction on the right has [MATH: \color{purple}2] shaded parts. Therefore, the fraction on the left is larger.

Item 10 — Tutorial: Comparing Fractions Using a Benchmark of One-Half

Content:
One way to compare fractions with no common numerators or denominators is to compare both fractions to [MATH: \dfrac{1}{2}.]

Content:
As an example, let's fill in the empty box in the comparison statement below:

Content:
[MATH: 00]

Content:
Now, we note the following:

Content:
- The fraction [MATH: \dfrac{3}{8}] is less than [MATH: \dfrac{1}{2}] because its numerator is less than one-half of its denominator.
- The fraction [MATH: \dfrac{5}{6}] is greater than [MATH: \dfrac{1}{2}] because its numerator is greater than one-half of its denominator.
- Since [MATH: \dfrac{3}{8}] is less than one-half yet [MATH: \dfrac{5}{6}] is greater than one-half, we conclude that [MATH: \dfrac{3}{8}] is less than [MATH: \dfrac{5}{6}.]

Content:
Therefore, the correct statement is the following:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{3}{8} < \dfrac{5}{6}]

Content:
We can verify this result using a fraction model:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d207548ca51ffe3979eb03c6cb7cf377]

Content:
Determining whether a fraction is greater than or less than [MATH: \dfrac{1}{2},] or which of two fractions is closer to [MATH: \dfrac{1}{2},] is known as comparing using the benchmark of [MATH: \dfrac{1}{2}.]

So, the correct answer is "I only."
